strengths: Introduces a large, well-engineered benchmark (DOMINO) with 35 tasks, 117K trajectories, 5 embodiments, and a principled three-tier dynamics taxonomy (predictable low-order, predictable high-order, stochastic/abrupt) parameterized by a scalar dynamics coefficient, enabling controlled difficulty scaling absent from prior static-world benchmarks.

Proposes a sensible and well-motivated metric suite (SR plus a continuous Manipulation Score with penalties for unsafe/erratic behavior) that goes beyond binary success, useful for future comparisons.

Extensive experimentation: systematic static-vs-dynamic comparisons across multiple VLA backbones, an informative oracle experiment isolating the role of ground-truth future trajectories, thorough ablations (history representation, prediction horizon, history length), cross-level/cross-coefficient generalization studies, and data-scaling analysis.

PUMA architecture is a reasonable, clearly described design (scene-centric historical optical flow + object-centric DINO-supervised future world queries) that adds negligible inference overhead (confirmed via latency benchmarking) while yielding consistent improvements over multiple strong baselines (π0, π0.5, OpenVLA-OFT, RDT, etc.) across dynamic interception and tracking task types.

Includes real-robot validation on a physical dual-arm platform with LoRA adaptation from simulation, showing sim-to-real transfer of the proposed dynamics-aware design, and demonstrates that dynamic training data can transfer beneficially back to static tasks, adding a useful empirical finding for the community.

Supplementary material is unusually thorough (per-task breakdowns for all 35 tasks across four transfer settings, failure-mode analysis, detailed construction pipeline for spatiotemporal synchronization, explicit limitations/future-work discussion).
weaknesses: Absolute performance remains very low even for the proposed method (17.2% SR on the main benchmark, single-digit-to-teens percentages on many individual tasks), which raises questions about whether the benchmark's difficulty/success criteria are well calibrated for meaningful method differentiation, and leaves unclear how close PUMA's gains bring the field to practically useful performance.

The synthetic data generation pipeline uses a kinematic 'stop-on-contact' simplification for object dynamics, and objects are effectively pre-scripted based on back-calculated timing; this idealizes the interception problem (e.g., no sensor noise in target velocity, no unmodeled contact physics before grasp) and may not fully capture real dynamic-manipulation challenges, a limitation the authors do acknowledge.

Real-world validation, while a plus, is limited in scope (5 tasks, 20 trials/task, only linear/Level-1-like dynamics generated via string-pulling), so it does not strongly test generalization to Level 2/3 or more naturalistic real dynamic disturbances (e.g., human-driven motion).

The technical novelty of PUMA is somewhat incremental: it combines existing building blocks (Farneback optical flow, GroundingDINO+SAM2, frozen DINO feature supervision, learnable query tokens) in a new but not conceptually deep way; the core idea of auxiliary future-feature prediction is similar in spirit to existing world-model-augmented VLA works (e.g., DreamVLA) cited by the authors, with the main claimed distinction being object-centric vs scene-centric prediction.

Some benchmark design choices (e.g., fixed α=0.1 as the primary evaluation setting throughout most experiments, task selection/criteria for success in stochastic Level-3 scenarios) are not deeply justified, and minor inconsistencies appear across tables/figures (e.g., slightly different π0.5/ACT numbers between Fig. 1 and Table 1).

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem for VLAs: manipulation of dynamically moving objects, with a clear formalization (POMDP) and principled dynamics-coefficient parameterization (DOMINO@α) that scales task difficulty in a controlled manner.

DOMINO is a large-scale, carefully engineered benchmark (117K trajectories, 35 tasks, 5 embodiments, three hierarchical dynamics levels, dynamic interception vs. tracking taxonomy) with a non-trivial data generation pipeline (dry-run + kinematic back-calculation + synchronized rollout) to solve the spatiotemporal synchronization problem.

Extensive baseline evaluation against many recent SOTA VLAs (OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, RDT, π0, π0.5, π0-FAST, VLA-Adapter, InternVLA-M1, Isaac-GR00T) with consistent re-implementation on a shared Qwen3-VL backbone for fairness.

Thorough ablation studies (history length, prediction horizon, flow vs. raw frames, co-training with static data, cross-level and cross-α generalization, data scaling) that support the design choices behind PUMA reasonably well.
Real-robot validation with sim-to-real LoRA adaptation, plus inference-latency/control-frequency analysis showing negligible overhead from the added dynamics-aware modules.
Useful auxiliary findings (Findings 1-3) connecting dynamic training to representation generalization for static tasks, which could be of independent interest to the community.
weaknesses: Absolute performance remains very low even for the proposed method (17.2% SR at the easiest Level 1 dynamics, dropping to single digits at Level 2/3), which raises doubts about whether the benchmark and method combination yields a compelling proof of concept for practical dynamic manipulation, beyond confirming that the problem is hard.

The technical novelty of PUMA is incremental: it largely combines existing ingredients (Farneback optical flow for history, DINO-feature cosine-similarity prediction akin to DreamVLA-style world queries, GroundingDINO+SAM2 for object grounding) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism; the paper's own related-work section positions it as an incremental step ('exploratory attempt') over DreamVLA and similar approaches.

Real-world validation is limited to 5 simple tasks with an artificial dynamic setup (objects pulled by transparent strings at controlled linear speeds), which does not convincingly demonstrate handling of the higher-order/stochastic dynamics (Level 2/3) that the paper emphasizes as key contributions in simulation; only 20 trials per task further limits statistical confidence.

The 'expert' trajectories in DOMINO are generated via scripted kinematic replay synchronized to a pre-recorded static execution time, rather than genuine closed-loop reactive teleoperation/policy; this may bias the dataset toward feed-forward interception patterns rather than true reactive dynamic behavior, potentially limiting how representative the benchmark is of real dynamic-manipulation challenges.

Reliance on multiple frozen off-the-shelf perception modules (GroundingDINO, SAM2, DINO) for constructing training supervision introduces additional failure points and dependency on open-vocabulary grounding quality that are not stress-tested (e.g., grounding failure rates, sensitivity to prompt parsing errors) despite claiming a 'no overhead at inference' benefit.

Baseline comparisons, while broad, are all fine-tuned under a fixed protocol on DOMINO; there is limited discussion of hyperparameter tuning fairness for baselines not natively using Qwen3-VL, and no comparison against other existing dynamic-manipulation approaches cited in related work ([60],[70]) despite explicitly critiquing them as 'restricted to simplified motion tasks.'

The paper's central claimed improvement (6.3% absolute SR gain) is modest in absolute terms and its practical significance is unclear given the overall low success rates across all methods, making it hard to assess whether the architectural contributions meaningfully close the static-to-dynamic performance gap highlighted in the introduction.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem (dynamic manipulation) with a large-scale, carefully engineered benchmark (DOMINO): 35 tasks, 5 embodiments, >110K trajectories, hierarchical difficulty levels (Level 1-3), and a well-motivated multi-dimensional evaluation protocol (SR + Manipulation Score with safety penalties) that goes beyond binary success.

The three-stage spatiotemporal synchronization data-generation pipeline (dry-run, kinematic back-calculation, synchronized rollout) is a sensible engineering solution to a genuinely hard data-collection problem, and is clearly documented with reproducible detail in the appendix.

PUMA is a reasonably motivated architecture: explicit optical-flow encoding of history (shown empirically to outperform raw-frame stacking) combined with object-centric future-state prediction via frozen DINO/GroundingDINO+SAM2 supervision, added with negligible inference overhead (only ~3-4% latency increase vs. backbone-only baselines).

Extensive experimentation: broad comparison against 10 SOTA VLA baselines, systematic ablations (history length, prediction horizon, historical representation choice, history-aware baseline comparison with ContextVLA), cross-difficulty-level transfer, data-scaling study, and out-of-distribution dynamic-coefficient generalization tests, most contained in a substantial supplementary section.

Includes real-world validation on a physical dual-arm platform with LoRA sim-to-real adaptation, showing consistent (though not dramatic in absolute terms) gains over baselines, which strengthens the practical relevance of the simulation findings.

Honest discussion of open challenges: the paper explicitly reports failure modes (reactive chasing, spatial-distribution overfitting, bimanual coordination failure) and outlines concrete future directions rather than overstating the solved nature of the problem.
weaknesses: Absolute performance remains low even for the proposed method (17.2% SR on Level 1, dropping further at Level 2/3), so while relative improvements are meaningful, the paper does not demonstrate that dynamic manipulation is close to being solved; most core results are restricted to the easiest Level 1 (constant-velocity) dynamics.

The expert-data generation procedure relies on a pre-computed, back-calculated synchronization between a static-scene motion plan and object trajectory rather than a genuinely closed-loop reactive policy; this raises a question about whether the 'expert' demonstrations encode true visual reactivity to motion or largely reproduce fixed trajectories that happen to align in time, which could affect how representative the learned behavior is of real reactive dynamic manipulation.

Real-robot evaluation, while a valuable addition, is limited to five tasks with objects pulled via strings at controlled speeds—an approximation of dynamic motion that may not capture the full complexity (noise, variable speed, occlusion patterns) of real dynamic environments; only 20 trials per task limits statistical confidence.

Generalization claims center mainly on cross-static/dynamic and cross-difficulty-level transfer on a single embodiment (Aloha-AgileX) for most core experiments; despite the dataset spanning 5 embodiments, cross-embodiment transfer of PUMA itself is not evaluated in the main results.

Some engineering choices (e.g., λ weighting, world-query count, optimal history/future window) appear tuned specifically for PUMA and are not clearly stress-tested for robustness across tasks or difficulty levels beyond the reported ablations, leaving some sensitivity questions about hyperparameter fragility.
